query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA, limited diffusion after casting produces a metastable mixture of solid-solution regions and intermetallic compounds. Subsequent controlled heat treatment induces diffusion‐driven phase partitioning such that protective alloying elements (e.g. Al and Gd) segregate to form a refined intermetallic network and localized compositional gradients. This evolution facilitates the formation of a continuous, adherent oxide scale (comprising e.g. Al2O3/MgO and possibly Gd oxides) during high-temperature exposure and minimizes micro-galvanic coupling, thereby reducing corrosion attack.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast Mg–Al–Cu–Zn–Gd high-entropy alloy displaying a non-equilibrium microstructure with mixed solid-solution and metastable intermetallic phases and an overall density below 6 g/cm3.
generation.intervention: A controlled post-casting annealing treatment (for example, heating at approximately 550°C for a fixed duration) designed to allow limited diffusion and phase reordering without reaching full equilibrium.
generation.conditions: Electrochemical corrosion tests performed in a 0.1 M NaCl solution at room temperature and high-temperature oxidation tests in air at 800–900°C.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution of the microstructure via diffusion‐driven phase transformation—specifically, the segregation of Al, Gd, and possibly Cu to grain boundaries and interphase regions—which promotes the formation of a finely distributed, protective intermetallic network and, later, a continuous passivating oxide layer.
generation.mechanism: Post solidification, the metastable state begins to evolve via atomic diffusion. The redistribution of elements leads to the stabilization of intermetallic phases that are richer in oxidation‐resistant elements. This reordering causes selective enrichment at the surface and at grain boundaries, where upon high-temperature exposure, the preferential formation of protective oxide films (such as Al2O3 and MgO) occurs. This passivation mitigates localized galvanic differences and enhances both corrosion resistance and oxidation behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast, non-equilibrated alloy, the heat-treated alloy is expected to exhibit a lower corrosion current density and improved oxide scale adhesion and integrity during high-temperature oxidation. Microstructural characterization should reveal a refined intermetallic network with enriched regions of Al and Gd at critical interfaces.
generation.baseline: As-cast Mg–Al–Cu–Zn–Gd lightweight HEA with a heterogeneous, non-equilibrium microstructure.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under processing conditions that maintain densities below 6 g/cm3 and where the differences in constituent properties favor stable intermetallic compound formation. It may not hold if the heat treatment results in excessive homogenization or if diffusion kinetics are too rapid, erasing the beneficial segregation.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative role of element segregation and phase evolution in promoting passivation is supported by related studies, the precise quantitative contributions of specific elements (e.g., Gd versus Cu) to the improved corrosion and oxidation behavior remain uncertain and warrant further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Mg–Al–Cu–Zn–Gd HEA samples. One set remains in the as-cast condition while the other is subjected to a controlled annealing treatment at 550°C for 10 hours under an inert atmosphere to provide the opportunity for controlled phase evolution. Both sets are then exposed to corrosion testing in 0.1 M NaCl at room temperature and to high-temperature oxidation testing in air at 850°C for a fixed duration.
measurements: Potentiodynamic polarization tests to determine corrosion current densities
Weight change measurements and visual/SEM assessment of oxide scale adhesion during oxidation
Microstructural analyses using SEM, TEM, and XRD to identify phase evolution and elemental segregation
Surface chemical composition analysis via XPS to verify formation of protective oxides
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., >20% reduction in corrosion current density and enhanced scale integrity) compared to the as-cast samples, or if microstructural and surface analyses fail to show targeted segregation or formation of a protective oxide layer, then the mechanistic hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, the association between thermal history and resultant phases and microstructures are investigated for the equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu system. By carefully controlling the thermal processing history of the system, the alloy was extensively evaluated and the following summarizes the key results: When prepared by arc melting and casting, this alloy system decomposes into a primary FCC phase resembling the Cantor alloy and a secondary FCC solid solution phase enriched with Cu. The primary and secondary FCC phases remain compositionally partitioned after high-temperature annealing, with no tendency towards homogenization. However, significant morphological evolution takes place resulting in the formation of a “lava-lamp” morphology that is characteristic of immiscible alloys. To this effect, it is postulated that the system forms a duplex microstructure owing to a monotectic reaction. The work further introduces a method applicable to HEA development, wherein controlled processing conditions dictate the most probable and stable composition. The aim of the present work is to investigate the influence of systematic variations in Mg content on the microstructure, mechanical properties, and corrosion behavior of these alloys. By characterizing the resulting intermetallic phases, grain refinement, and passive film formation, this study identified how processing and composition synergistically affect the corrosion resistance and mechanical performance. This work offers new insights into the design of corrosion-resistant, high-strength materials and represents a novel extension of compositionally complex alloy design to Mg-rich systems.

Lightweight complex concentrated alloys (LWCCA), composed of elements with low density, have become a great area of interest due to the high demand in a large number of applications. Previous research on LWCCAs was focused on high entropy multicomponent alloy systems that provide low density and high capability of solid solution formation. Present research introduces two alloy systems (Al-Cu-Si-Zn-Mg and Al-Mn-Zn-Mg-Si) that contain readily available and inexpensive starting materials and have potential for solid solution formation structures. For the selection of appropriate compositions, authors applied semi-empirical criteria and optimization software. Specialized modeling software (MatCalc) was used to determine probable alloy structures by CALPHAD, non-equilibrium solidification and kinetic simulations. The selected alloys were prepared in an induction furnace. Specimens were heat treated to provide stable structures. Physicochemical, microstructural, and mechanical characterization was performed for the selected alloy compositions.
